title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
text:
Academic expertise


Figure A1: Level of education and relation to portfolio









Figure A1. Level of education and relation to portfolio (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
General pattern: Nearly all ministers hold at least a graduate-level degree (499/507, 98.4%). Within this group, PhD holders account for 27.8% of all ministers (141/507), postgraduate (non-PhD) degree holders for 10.8% (55/507), and graduate-only degree holders for the remaining 59.8% (303/507). Only 1.6% (8/507) reached secondary education alone, and no minister shows primary, non-university higher, or no formal education. This matches the standard finding in the literature, which typically stops at this level of description (“ministers are highly credentialed”).
With portfolio relation: Overall, only 60.0% of ministers (304/507) hold an educational background related to their portfolio; the remaining 40.0% do not, despite the near-universal presence of graduate-level credentials. Relatedness is not monotonic with educational level: it is highest among postgraduate (non-PhD) degree holders (80.0%, 44/55), intermediate among PhD holders (63.8%, 90/141), and lowest among graduate-only degree holders (56.1%, 170/303). All 8 ministers with secondary education alone show no portfolio relation. This is the first indication, still at the raw-indicator level, that credential level alone is a poor proxy for portfolio-specific expertise: the highest observed relatedness rate does not correspond to the highest educational level.
 #### Figure A2: Field of education, by level









Figure A2. Field of education, undergraduate and postgraduate (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
At the undergraduate level, Law is by far the most common field of education (38.5%, 195/507), followed by Engineering (22.5%, 114/507) and Economics (19.9%, 101/507). Social Sciences (6.7%, 34/507), Humanities (3.4%, 17/507) and Military studies (2.8%, 14/507) are considerably less frequent, and Management is nearly absent as a first degree (0.4%, 2/507). Only 1.6% of ministers (8/507) report no undergraduate field.
At the postgraduate level, the dominant pattern is simply the absence of further education: 54.0% of ministers (274/507) hold no postgraduate degree at all. Among those who do, Law (12.8% of all ministers, 65/507) and Economics (12.2%, 62/507) remain the largest fields, followed by Engineering (6.1%, 31/507) and Social Sciences (5.5%, 28/507). Management, nearly absent at undergraduate level, becomes proportionally more present at postgraduate level (2.8%, 14/507, against 0.4% at undergraduate), consistent with management training being acquired mainly through postgraduate qualifications rather than as a first degree.
This is the level at which the existing literature typically stops: reporting which fields are more or less frequent among ministers, without asking whether those fields are actually relevant to the portfolios ministers go on to hold.



Figure A3: Field of education, by relation to the portfolio









Figure A3. Field of the highest degree attained, by relation to the portfolio (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507). Bars show the field of each minister’s highest educational qualification; segments show whether, and at which level, any of the minister’s education is related to the substantive area of their portfolio (graduate, postgraduate non-PhD, or PhD).
Field of the highest degree, by relation to the portfolio: Military education remains the field most consistently tied to portfolio relevance, and now we can be precise about where: 92.9% of ministers with military as their highest field (13/14) show that relevance at the graduate level itself, with no cases at postgraduate or PhD level, consistent with military training as a single, self-contained qualification track.
Law and Economics continue to diverge sharply. Law shows 39.4% no relation (71/180), 37.2% related at graduate level (67/180), 12.2% at postgraduate non-PhD level (22/180), and 11.1% at PhD level (20/180); relatedness is spread fairly evenly across all three related tiers. Economics shows 23.9% no relation (27/113), 38.1% related at graduate level (43/113), only 12.4% at postgraduate non-PhD level (14/113), but 25.7% at PhD level (29/113), meaning that when an Economics background is related to the portfolio beyond the first degree, it is disproportionately a doctorate rather than a non-PhD postgraduate qualification.
Engineering keeps the lowest overall relatedness among fields with substantial N (47.1%, 40/85), with the disaggregation showing that what little postgraduate-level relation exists is concentrated at PhD level (12.9%, 11/85) rather than non-PhD postgraduate (3.5%, 3/85).
The disaggregation is most informative for Medicine and Formal Sciences. What earlier appeared as postgraduate-level relatedness for these two fields turns out to be entirely PhD-driven: Medicine shows 0% at postgraduate non-PhD level and 50.0% at PhD level (8/16); Formal Sciences shows 0% at postgraduate non-PhD level and 73.3% at PhD level (11/15). In both fields, relatedness beyond the first degree is acquired exclusively through doctoral training, not through non-PhD postgraduate qualifications.
Social Sciences remains the field with the lowest overall relatedness among the more frequent fields (73.9% not related, 34/46), split evenly between postgraduate non-PhD (4.3%, 2/46) and PhD level (10.9%, 5/46).
As an internal consistency check: the four column totals in A3 (203 not related, 170 related at graduate level, 44 related at postgraduate non-PhD level, 90 related at PhD level) match exactly the marginal distribution of edu_level_related reported for the full sample, and the 8 ministers with no field (“none”) are all classified as not related, consistent with the 8 secondary-only ministers identified in A1.



Figure A4: Academic dimension









Figure A4. Distribution of academic expertise (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
The aggregated academic dimension distributes as follows: 40.0% of ministers (203/507) show no academic expertise, 39.1% (198/507) some, and 20.9% (106/507) ample. Read jointly with Figure A3, this trichotomous summary is consistent with the field-by-relatedness pattern already described: given that only 60.0% of ministers hold any portfolio-related education (Figure A1), and that among these a large share is related only at the graduate level, ample academic expertise, the top category of the scale, is reached by roughly one in five ministers, while a comparable share (40.0%) reaches none at all.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
text:
Occupational Dimension

Figure A5: Prior occupation, by relation to the portfolio









Figure A5. Prior occupational background, by occupational expertise (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507). Bars show ministers’ occupational background prior to appointment, aggregated into nine career families (expertise_Job_type_agg); segments show the level of occupational expertise (expertise_Job: none/some/ample) associated with that background.
Prior occupation: Political careers are by far the most common occupational background among Portuguese ministers (43.0%, 218/507), roughly two and a half times more frequent than the next largest category, Academic (16.2%, 82/507). State careers (13.4%, 68/507), Business (12.2%, 62/507) and Legal (9.7%, 49/507) form a middle tier, while Military and Professional backgrounds are each rare (1.6%, 8/507 each), and Civil society and Economist are the smallest categories (1.2%, 6/507 each).
Prior occupation, by relation to the portfolio: Crossing occupational background with occupational expertise shows that the most common pathway into ministerial office is not the one most likely to generate high occupational expertise. Political careers, despite accounting for 43.0% of all ministers, generate ample occupational expertise in only 36.2% of cases (79/218), with 39.9% reaching only some (87/218) and 23.9% none (52/218). By contrast, considerably less frequent backgrounds show markedly higher ample rates: State careers reach ample in 57.4% of cases (39/68), Academic careers in 56.1% (46/82), and Military careers in 75.0% (6/8, though this last figure rests on a very small N and should be read with caution). Economist shows the highest point estimate of all (66.7%, 4/6) but is based on only 6 cases.
Business and Legal occupy an intermediate, fairly flat position: both split close to evenly across the three levels (Business: 32.3% none, 32.3% some, 35.5% ample; Legal: 30.6% none, 30.6% some, 38.8% ample), with no strong concentration at either extreme. Civil society and Professional, the smallest categories alongside Military and Economist, are concentrated at the some level (50.0% and 37.5% respectively) rather than at none or ample.
Overall, across all 507 ministers, 22.3% show no occupational expertise (113), 34.3% some (174), and 43.4% ample (220). Political careers underperform this overall ample rate (36.2% vs. 43.4%), which is notable precisely because they are the modal pathway into office: the largest single route into the ministerial elite is not the one generating the highest levels of portfolio-relevant occupational expertise.



Figure A6: Occupational dimension









Figure A6. Distribution of occupational expertise (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
The aggregated occupational dimension shows 22.3% of ministers (113/507) with no occupational expertise, 34.3% (174/507) with some, and 43.4% (220/507) with ample, the highest ample share of the three dimensions. As already noted in relation to Figure A5, this overall distribution is not driven by the modal occupational background: political careers, which account for 43.0% of all ministers, generate ample occupational expertise in only 36.2% of cases, below the 43.4% ample rate for the sample as a whole.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
text:
Managerial Dimension

Figure A7: Managerial experience sector









Figure A7. Sector of prior managerial experience (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
Prior managerial experience among Portuguese ministers is heavily concentrated in the public sector: 75.3% (382/507) held managerial experience exclusively in the public sector, compared to only 1.4% (7/507) exclusively in the private sector and 8.1% (41/507) in both sectors. A further 15.2% (77/507) report no prior managerial experience at all. This sectoral concentration mirrors the broader recruitment pattern already noted for occupational background (Figure A5), where political and state careers, both public-sector-anchored, together account for more than half of all ministers.



Figure A8: Managerial experience sector, by level of managerial expertise









Figure A8. Sector of managerial experience, by managerial expertise (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
Crossing sector of managerial experience with the level of managerial expertise shows that experience in the public sector, and especially in both sectors combined, is what converts into higher managerial expertise. Among the 41 ministers with experience in both the public and private sectors, 75.6% (31/41) reach ample managerial expertise, the highest ample rate of any sector category. Ministers with public-sector-only experience reach ample in 45.3% of cases (173/382), close to the 41.0% ample rate for the sample as a whole (Figure A10), while the small group with private-sector-only experience splits between some (42.9%, 3/7) and ample (57.1%, 4/7). By construction, all 77 ministers with no prior managerial experience score none on the managerial dimension.



Figure A9: Occupational background, by managerial expertise









Figure A9. Occupational background, by managerial expertise (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
State careers generate the highest rate of ample managerial expertise among occupational backgrounds with substantial N (52.9%, 36/68), followed by Political careers (45.0%, 98/218) and Business (45.2%, 28/62); State and Political careers are both concentrated in the public sector, consistent with the sector pattern already described in A7/A8, where public-sector experience converts into ample managerial expertise at a markedly higher rate than private-sector-only experience. Economist (66.7%, 4/6) and Military (37.5%, 3/8) show still higher or comparable point estimates but rest on very small N and should be read with caution. Professional stands out as the clearest exception to the public-sector pattern: despite a small N (8), 87.5% (7/8) reach only some and none reach ample, the only occupational category with a 0% ample rate. Academic careers show a comparatively low ample rate (24.4%, 20/82) despite the discipline’s frequent public-sector orientation, indicating that managerial expertise is not simply a byproduct of sector exposure but depends on the specific type of managerial role held.



Figure A10: Managerial dimension









Figure A10. Distribution of managerial expertise (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
The aggregated managerial dimension shows 15.2% of ministers (77/507) with no managerial expertise, 43.8% (222/507) with some, and 41.0% (208/507) with ample. Of the three dimensions, managerial expertise has the lowest share at none (15.2%, against 22.3% for occupational and 40.0% for academic) and a substantial ample share (41.0%), only slightly below the 43.4% ample rate of the occupational dimension. As already shown in Figures A7 and A8, this reflects the near-universal (84.8%) prior managerial experience among Portuguese ministers, concentrated overwhelmingly in the public sector, and the fact that public-sector and mixed-sector experience convert into ample managerial expertise at comparatively high rates.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
section: Figure B2: Correlations among academic, occupational, and managerial expertise
text:
Figure B2: Correlations among academic, occupational, and managerial expertise









Figure B2. Polychoric correlations among academic, occupational, and managerial expertise (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
Academic-occupational. The polychoric correlation is moderate (r = 0.45), the strongest of the three pairs. The co-occurrence table shows a clear positive gradient: ample occupational expertise rises from 27.1% among ministers with no academic expertise to 43.9% (some) and 73.6% (ample). The association is real but far from a substitution: 27.1% of ministers with no academic expertise still reach ample occupational expertise, and 5.7% of ministers with ample academic expertise remain at none on the occupational side. The two dimensions correlate, but neither is reducible to the other.
Academic-managerial. The polychoric correlation is weak (r = 0.12), the weakest of the three pairs. The co-occurrence table is comparatively flat: ample managerial expertise rises only modestly across academic levels (34.5%, 44.4%, 47.2%), and the share with no managerial expertise barely moves (16.7%, 14.6%, 13.2%). Academic and managerial expertise behave as largely independent, distinct forms of competence, consistent with managerial expertise’s transversal, non-domain-specific character (Paper 1).
Occupational-managerial. The polychoric correlation is moderate (r = 0.33), between the other two pairs. Ample managerial expertise rises from 23.9% (no occupational expertise) to 35.6% (some) and 54.1% (ample), while the share with no managerial expertise falls from 27.4% to 10.0% over the same range. The association is closer than academic-managerial but still leaves substantial independent variation.
Across the three pairs, the pattern is one of moderate and uneven association, not full redundancy or full independence: strongest between academic and occupational expertise, weakest between academic and managerial, intermediate between occupational and managerial. This does not support treating educational and occupational credentials as interchangeable proxies for a single construct, nor does it support treating managerial expertise as redundant with the other two.
As an internal consistency check: the row totals in both t_AcaJob and t_AcaManag (203 none, 198 some, 106 ample) match each other, since both share the same Academic marginal; and the row totals in t_JobManag (113 none, 174 some, 220 ample) match exactly the overall occupational expertise distribution already reported in A6.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
section: Figure C1: Multidimensionality of the expertise space (Eigenvalues)
text:
Figure C1: Multidimensionality of the expertise space (Eigenvalues)









Figure C1. Eigenvalues / percentage of inertia by axis, MCA of academic, occupational, and managerial expertise (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507).
The first axis accounts for only 24.96% of total inertia, far short of what a single dominant dimension would require. The remaining axes decline gradually rather than dropping off sharply: 18.45%, 17.08%, 14.90%, 14.73%, and 9.88%. Four axes are needed to reach 75.4% of total inertia. If academic, occupational, and managerial expertise were redundant, collapsible onto one latent trait, the first axis would concentrate most of the inertia and the rest would be negligible; instead, inertia is distributed fairly evenly across several axes. This directly tests, and does not support, the assumption built into unidimensional or additive indices: the expertise space is genuinely multidimensional, not reducible to a single technocratic gradient.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
section: Figure C2: Dimensional structure of the axes (eta²)
text:
Figure C2: Dimensional structure of the axes (eta²)









Figure C2. Association (η²) between each expertise dimension and each MCA axis (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507). Axis n corresponds to MCA Dimension n; terminology follows the program convention (see glossary).
Each axis is structured by a different dominant dimension, and the pattern sharpens as one moves past the first axis. Axis 1 combines occupational (η² = 0.67) and academic (η² = 0.50) expertise, a general gradient of accumulation, with managerial contributing more moderately (η² = 0.33). Axis 2 is occupational-specific (η² = 0.57), with managerial secondary (η² = 0.38) and academic weak (η² = 0.16). Axis 3 is academic-specific (η² = 0.65) and essentially orthogonal to occupational (η² = 0.01), the clearest case of dimensional separation in the whole space. Axis 4 is managerial-specific (η² = 0.54), with occupational nearly absent (η² = 0.05). Axis 5 is more mixed, with moderate loadings from all three (Job = 0.38, Manag = 0.31, Acad = 0.19), consistent with a residual axis. Taken together, each of the three dimensions has at least one axis on which it dominates and on which the others are weak or negligible, evidence that academic, occupational, and managerial expertise are not collapsing into one another even where they share a common general axis.

Step 4: Cluster profiles by expertise dimension

Figure C4: Cluster profile, by expertise dimension









Figure C4. Mean expertise level per dimension, by cluster (Portugal, ministerial appointments, N=507). Clusters identified by number only; substantive labels are assigned in Step 5, after inspecting this profile.
The mean score on each dimension (1 = none, 2 = some, 3 = ample) defines each cluster substantively. C1 Polivalent Experts (N=91, 17.9%) is high on all three dimensions (Academic 3.00, Occupational 2.71, Managerial 2.55), the only cluster strong across the board. C2 Executive Politicians (N=158, 31.2%, the largest cluster) is dominated by managerial expertise (3.00, the maximum), with occupational moderately high (2.35) and academic the weakest of the three (1.56). C3 Political Generalists (N=81, 16.0%) is flat and moderate across all three dimensions (2.00, 2.14, 2.00), with no dimension standing out. C4 Academic Specialists (N=77, 15.2%) is defined less by academic strength in absolute terms (1.74, actually slightly below occupational at 1.88) than by the near-total absence of managerial expertise (1.00, the floor: every minister in this cluster scores none on managerial); relative to that floor, academic and occupational are the retained dimensions, hence the label. C5 Generalist Politicians (N=100, 19.7%) is the mirror case of low academic expertise (1.02, essentially floor), with occupational (1.84) and managerial (2.00) both moderate.
No single configuration dominates the ministerial population: the largest cluster accounts for less than a third of cases, and the other four range narrowly between 15% and 20%. This plurality would not be visible under a unidimensional or additive index, which by construction produces a single ranked continuum rather than discrete, qualitatively distinct configurations. The recurrence of clusters combining high managerial with low academic (C2), and low managerial with modest academic and occupational (C4), in particular, shows configurations that a “more expertise is always better” index would score similarly, low or middling, while in fact they represent qualitatively different resource profiles.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
section: Figure C5: Clusters vs. logical types
text:
Figure C5: Clusters vs. logical types
The correspondence is strong and clean. Each empirical cluster is composed almost exclusively of a small, coherent subset of logical types sharing a common anchor dimension; none of the nine logical types is scattered across unrelated clusters.
C1 Polivalent Experts is built entirely from logical types that include ample academic expertise: pure academic (13.2%), academic-occupational (31.9%), academic-managerial (11.0%), and integrated expertise, ample on all three (44.0%, nearly half the cluster). No minister in this cluster falls outside these four academic-anchored types.
C2 Executive Politicians splits exactly between the two logical types that include ample managerial expertise: pure managerial (50.0%) and occupational-managerial (50.0%). Every minister in this cluster has ample managerial expertise; the cluster differs internally only in whether occupational expertise also reaches ample.
C3 Political Generalists, C4 Academic Specialists, and C5 Generalist Politicians are dominated by ministers who reach ample on no dimension at all: partial expertise accounts for 65.4%, 41.6%, and 77.0% of each cluster respectively, and C4 additionally contains 23.4% with no expertise on any dimension, the only cluster where this type appears at meaningful scale. Where ample does appear in these three clusters, it is occupational (34.6% in C3, 16.9% in C4, 22.0% in C5) or, in C4 only, academic or academic-occupational (6.5% and 11.7%); managerial never reaches ample in any of the three, consistent with the near-zero managerial means already noted for C4 and C5.
Two conclusions follow. First, the empirical typology recovers the structure predicted by the logical typology: clusters anchored in academic ample (C1) and managerial ample (C2) map cleanly onto the corresponding logical types, external validation of the clustering solution. Second, the empirical typology adds resolution that the logical typology, built only from ample/not-ample thresholds, cannot provide on its own: three of the five clusters (C3, C4, C5) fall largely within the single residual category “partial expertise,” yet MCA and HCPC differentiate them clearly: a flat, moderate profile (C3), a profile anchored in the absence of managerial expertise (C4), and a profile anchored in the absence of academic expertise (C5). This is precisely the descriptive gain a graduated, multidimensional measure offers over a binary or purely deductive one.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
text:
Academic expertise


Figure A1: Level of education and relation to portfolio









Figure A1. Level of education and relation to portfolio (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415).
General pattern: Spanish ministers show a similarly high level of educational attainment to their Portuguese counterparts, though with a somewhat longer tail below graduate level. PhD holders account for 28.7% of all ministers (119/415), postgraduate (non-PhD) degree holders for 13.7% (57/415), and graduate-only degree holders for 54.7% (227/415). A small residual falls below graduate level: 1.9% (8/415) with secondary education only and 1.0% (4/415) with primary education only, the latter a category entirely absent from the Portuguese sample. Overall, 97.1% of Spanish ministers hold at least a graduate degree, close to but slightly below Portugal’s 98.4%.
With portfolio relation: Overall relatedness is somewhat lower in Spain than in Portugal (55.4%, 230/415, against 60.0% in Portugal). Unlike Portugal, where relatedness followed a non-monotonic, “hump-shaped” pattern (highest among postgraduate non-PhD holders at 80.0%, then PhD at 63.8%, then graduate-only at 56.1%), Spain shows a clean monotonic increase with educational level: 53.7% among graduate-only degree holders, 59.6% among postgraduate non-PhD holders, and 62.2% among PhD holders. Both countries agree that secondary-only education carries zero portfolio relation (0/8 in Spain, 0/8 in Portugal); Spain’s four primary-only ministers show the same pattern (0/4 related). The cross-country contrast is therefore not in direction (education level modestly favors relatedness in both cases) but in shape and magnitude: Portugal’s peak (80.0% at postgraduate non-PhD level) is considerably steeper than Spain’s ceiling (62.2% at PhD level), suggesting a less pronounced credential-relatedness gradient in the Spanish case.



Figure A2: Field of education, by level









Figure A2. Field of education, undergraduate and postgraduate (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415).
At the undergraduate level, Law dominates even more heavily in Spain than in Portugal: 56.4% of ministers (234/415), against 38.5% in Portugal. Economics follows at 17.1% (71/415), broadly comparable to Portugal’s 19.9%. The most striking divergence is Engineering, Portugal’s second-largest undergraduate field (22.5%), which is comparatively marginal in Spain (6.5%, 27/415). Natural Sciences, negligible in Portugal (0.8%), is noticeably more present in Spain (4.3%, 18/415), and the share reporting no undergraduate field is roughly double (3.1%, 13/415, against 1.6% in Portugal).
At the postgraduate level, the dominant pattern again is the absence of further education, slightly more pronounced than in Portugal (56.6% with no postgraduate degree, 235/415, against 54.0%). Among those who do continue, Law and Economics are essentially tied (14.7%, 61/415, and 14.9%, 62/415, respectively), with Economics marginally ahead, unlike Portugal, where Law led at every stage (12.8% against Economics’ 12.2%). Engineering’s postgraduate share is much lower in Spain (2.2%) than in Portugal (6.1%), consistent with its smaller undergraduate footprint. Management, a small but non-zero postgraduate niche in Portugal (2.8%), is entirely absent in the Spanish sample (0%), at both undergraduate and postgraduate level.



Figure A3: Field of education, by relation to the portfolio









Figure A3. Field of the highest degree attained, by relation to the portfolio (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415). Bars show the field of each minister’s highest educational qualification; segments show whether, and at which level, any of the minister’s education is related to the substantive area of their portfolio (graduate, postgraduate non-PhD, or PhD).
Military education again shows the highest relatedness of any field, and again entirely at graduate level: 100% (3/3) in Spain, against 92.9% (13/14) in Portugal, both on small N.
Law and Economics, the two largest fields, diverge from each other differently than in Portugal. Law shows 41.4% no relation (84/203), close to Portugal’s 39.4%, but the distribution of related cases is more concentrated at the first-degree level (40.4% graduate-related) with a nearly empty postgraduate non-PhD tier (2.0%, against Portugal’s 12.2%) and a larger PhD-related share (16.3%, against 11.1%). Economics shows a higher no-relation share than in Portugal (31.1% against 23.9%) and a markedly flatter spread across the three related tiers (23.3% graduate, 21.1% postgraduate, 24.4% PhD), instead of Portugal’s graduate-heavy pattern (38.1% graduate against only 12.4% postgraduate).
Engineering keeps a similarly low overall relatedness in both countries (45.2% not related in Spain against 47.1% in Portugal), with postgraduate-level relation concentrated at PhD level in both cases (16.1% against 3.2% non-PhD postgraduate in Spain; 12.9% against 3.5% in Portugal). Medicine and Social Sciences diverge more sharply: Medicine shows markedly lower relatedness in Spain (45.5% related overall, against 81.2% in Portugal, both on small N and to be read with caution), while Social Sciences shows markedly higher relatedness in Spain (48.5% related, against 26.1% in Portugal). Natural Sciences, too small to assess in Portugal (N=1), is analyzable in Spain (N=18) and shows very low relatedness (83.3% not related). Humanities shows lower relatedness in Spain (60.0% not related, against 38.5% in Portugal).
As an internal consistency check: the four column totals in A3 (185 not related, 127 related at graduate level, 29 at postgraduate non-PhD level, 74 at PhD level) match exactly the marginal distribution of edu_level_related for the full sample, and the 12 ministers with no field (“none”) are all classified as not related, consistent with the 8 secondary-only and 4 primary-only ministers identified in A1 (8+4=12).



Figure A4: Academic dimension









Figure A4. Distribution of academic expertise (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415).
The aggregated academic dimension shows 44.8% of ministers (186/415) with no academic expertise, 34.7% (144/415) with some, and 20.5% (85/415) with ample. The ample share is nearly identical to Portugal’s (20.5% against 20.9%): both countries produce roughly one academically ample minister in five. The difference lies at the bottom of the scale: Spain has a markedly higher none share (44.8% against Portugal’s 40.0%) and a correspondingly lower some share (34.7% against 39.1%), consistent with Spain’s somewhat lower overall portfolio-relatedness already noted in Figure A1 (55.4% against 60.0%).

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
text:
Occupational Dimension

Figure A5: Prior occupation, by relation to the portfolio









Figure A5. Prior occupational background, by occupational expertise (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415). Bars show ministers’ occupational background prior to appointment, aggregated into nine career families (expertise_Job_type_agg); segments show the level of occupational expertise (expertise_Job: none/some/ample) associated with that background.
DATA GAP, not drafted: the underlying variable (expertise_Job_type_agg, the classification into nine occupational-career families) is unmapped for 100% of Spanish cases (415/415 “UNMAPPED - review”). It is not possible to describe which prior occupation is modal, nor whether it translates into higher occupational expertise, until this variable is coded. Pending recoding before this block can be drafted.



Figure A6: Occupational dimension









Figure A6. Distribution of occupational expertise (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415).
The aggregated occupational dimension shows 47.5% of ministers (197/415) with no occupational expertise, only 1.4% (6/415) with some, and 51.1% (212/415) with ample. This is a strikingly bimodal distribution: ministers split almost evenly between the two extremes, with the intermediate category nearly empty. This contrasts sharply with Portugal’s much more graduated spread (22.3% none, 34.3% some, 43.4% ample). Given that the underlying occupational-family variable is unmapped for Spain (see Figure A5), this near-absence of the “some” category should be read with some caution: it may reflect a genuine substantive feature of Spanish ministerial recruitment, but it could also be sensitive to how “some” is triggered at the coding stage, which cannot currently be cross-checked against the raw occupational categories. To confirm by the country-expert once the coding underlying A5 is complete.

Figure A10: Managerial dimension









Figure A10. Distribution of managerial expertise (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415).
The aggregated managerial dimension shows 53.3% of ministers (221/415) with no managerial expertise, only 3.1% (13/415) with some, and 43.6% (181/415) with ample. As with the occupational dimension (Figure A6), this is a strongly bimodal distribution, and it contrasts even more sharply with Portugal, where none was the smallest category (15.2%) and some the largest (43.8%): in Spain the ranking is reversed at the bottom, with none far more common than some. The ample share is comparable across countries (43.6% Spain against 41.0% Portugal): both countries generate ample managerial expertise in roughly two out of five ministers, but Spain reaches that ample rate from a much larger pool of ministers with no managerial experience at all, rather than through a broad middle tier. As with A6, the missing raw sector variable (A7/A8) means the substantive drivers of this bimodality cannot currently be unpacked further.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
section: Figure B2: Correlations among academic, occupational, and managerial expertise
text:
Figure B2: Correlations among academic, occupational, and managerial expertise









Figure B2. Polychoric correlations among academic, occupational, and managerial expertise (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415).
Academic-occupational. The polychoric correlation is moderate (r = 0.42), close to Portugal’s 0.45 and the strongest pair in both countries. The gradient is positive: ample occupational expertise rises from 34.4% (Academic none) to 61.8% (some) to 69.4% (ample). The discordant corners reveal an important cross-country difference: the none/ample corner is similar to Portugal’s (34.4% against 27.1%), but the ample/none corner is far larger in Spain: 29.4% of ministers with ample academic expertise show no occupational expertise at all, against only 5.7% in Portugal. Where Portugal’s association held strongly at the top and loosened only at the bottom, Spain’s association is more symmetrically loose at both extremes.
Academic-managerial. The polychoric correlation is weak (r = 0.20), slightly stronger than Portugal’s 0.12 but still one of the two weakest pairs, together with occupational-managerial below. The gradient is modest (36.0% → 46.5% → 55.3% ample managerial expertise across academic levels). The ample/none corner is again far larger than in Portugal: 44.7% of academically ample ministers have no managerial expertise, against 13.2% in Portugal, a substantial cross-country gap. Spain’s most academically credentialed ministers are markedly less likely to also carry managerial experience than Portugal’s.
Occupational-managerial. The polychoric correlation is weak (r = 0.19), notably weaker than Portugal’s 0.33, where this pair was the second-strongest. The gradient across the some row (66.7% none / 33.3% some / 0.0% ample) should not be read as a substantive dip: it rests on only 6 cases, the same 6 ministers flagged in Figure A6 as the entire some-occupational category, and is noise rather than signal. Reading only the none and ample rows, ample managerial expertise rises from 38.1% (Job none) to 50.0% (Job ample), a real but modest gradient, and the ample/none corner is large (47.2%, against Portugal’s 10.0%).
Taken together, Spain’s polychoric matrix has a different shape from Portugal’s. In Portugal, the three pairs were graded: academic-occupational strongest (0.45), occupational-managerial intermediate (0.33), academic-managerial weakest (0.12). In Spain, academic-occupational is again clearly the strongest (0.42), but the other two pairs are close to tied and both weak (0.20 and 0.19): managerial expertise is roughly equally distant from both other dimensions, rather than closer to occupational as in Portugal. If anything, this gives even stronger support in the Spanish data than in the Portuguese data for treating managerial expertise as a genuinely independent dimension, not redundant with either of the other two.
As an internal consistency check: the row totals in both t_AcaJob and t_AcaManag (186 none, 144 some, 85 ample) match each other and the A4 marginal; the row totals in t_JobManag (197 none, 6 some, 212 ample) match exactly the overall occupational expertise distribution already reported in A6.

section: Figure C1: Multidimensionality of the expertise space (Eigenvalues)
text:
Figure C1: Multidimensionality of the expertise space (Eigenvalues)









Figure C1. Eigenvalues / percentage of inertia by axis, MCA of academic, occupational, and managerial expertise (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415).
The first axis accounts for 23.40% of total inertia, close to Portugal’s 24.96% and, as in Portugal, far short of what a single dominant dimension would require. The remaining axes decline gradually (20.95%, 16.05%, 15.60%, 13.12%, 10.88%), and four axes are needed to reach 76.0% of total inertia, matching Portugal’s four-axes-to-75.4% threshold almost exactly. If anything, Spain’s inertia is even more evenly spread at the top than Portugal’s: the gap between the first and second axes is only 2.45 points in Spain (23.40 against 20.95), against 6.51 points in Portugal (24.96 against 18.45). This reinforces, if anything slightly more strongly than in Portugal, the conclusion that the expertise space is genuinely multidimensional rather than reducible to a single technocratic gradient.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
section: Figure C2: Dimensional structure of the axes (eta²)
text:
Figure C2: Dimensional structure of the axes (eta²)









Figure C2. Association (η²) between each expertise dimension and each MCA axis (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415). Axis n corresponds to MCA Dimension n; terminology follows the program convention (see glossary).
Axis 1 combines Academic (η² = 0.58) and Occupational (η² = 0.56), almost exactly tied, with Managerial weaker (η² = 0.26); Portugal’s Axis 1 was similarly occupational-academic, though there Occupational led more clearly (0.67 against 0.50). Axis 2 combines Occupational (0.56) and Managerial (0.52), both strong and nearly tied, with Academic weak (0.18): Portugal’s Axis 2 was also occupational-led (0.57) but with a considerably weaker managerial loading (0.38), so Spain’s second axis reads more clearly as a joint occupational-managerial axis than Portugal’s. Axis 3 is academic-specific (η² = 0.83) and essentially orthogonal to both other dimensions (Job = 0.10, Manag = 0.04): an even cleaner separation than Portugal’s Axis 3, which isolated academic from occupational (η² = 0.01) but still carried a non-trivial managerial loading (0.37). Axis 4 is managerial-specific (η² = 0.79), with academic and occupational both negligible (0.08 and 0.07): again a cleaner separation than Portugal’s Axis 4 (0.54, with academic non-negligible at 0.30). Axis 5 is mixed, dominated by Occupational (0.43) and Managerial (0.32) with Academic weak (0.04), a residual axis in both countries. Overall, each dimension again has at least one axis on which it dominates and the others are weak, as in Portugal, but Spain’s dimension-specific axes (3 and 4) show sharper, more orthogonal separation than Portugal’s equivalent axes.

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
text:
Configurations of expertise (clusters)

Step 1: Automatic (data-driven) solution

Figure C3: Cluster sizes (automatic solution)









Figure C3. Size of the clusters retained by the automatic (data-driven) HCPC solution (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415).
Unlike Portugal, where the unconstrained automatic solution returned four clusters (later refined to five for theoretical alignment), Spain’s automatic solution already returns five clusters directly, with no forcing needed: 178 (42.9%), 11 (2.7%), 6 (1.5%), 136 (32.8%), and 84 (20.2%) ministers. The distribution is considerably more skewed than Portugal’s final five-cluster solution (which ranged narrowly between 15% and 20% for its smaller four clusters): Spain has two very small clusters (11 and 6 cases) alongside three much larger ones. Given that the automatic solution already yields five clusters unforced, Steps 2 and 3 (theory-driven forcing) are not run for Spain; the automatic solution is adopted directly as cluster_final.




Steps 2 & 3 — Data Manager task only (theory-driven alternative, if applicable)



Step 4: Cluster profiles by expertise dimension

Figure C4: Cluster profile, by expertise dimension









Figure C4. Mean expertise level per dimension, by cluster (Spain, ministerial appointments, N=415). Clusters identified by number only; substantive labels are assigned in Step 5, after inspecting this profile.
Three of the five clusters are defined almost purely by academic expertise level, each corresponding to exactly one rung of the trichotomous scale: Cluster 1 (N=178, 42.9%) is 100% academic-none (mean 1.00), with low-to-moderate occupational (1.69) and managerial (1.75) expertise; Cluster 4 (N=136, 32.8%) is 100% academic-some (mean 2.00), with moderately high occupational (2.26) and low-to-moderate managerial (1.99) expertise; Cluster 5 (N=84, 20.2%) is 100% academic-ample (mean 3.00), with moderately high occupational (2.40) and managerial (2.12) expertise, the closest Spanish analogue to Portugal’s Polivalent Experts, though with visibly less stacking: Portugal’s equivalent cluster reached 2.71 (occupational) and 2.55 (managerial), both closer to the ample ceiling than Spain’s 2.40 and 2.12.
The remaining two clusters are small and structured differently: instead of combining across dimensions, they isolate the rare some cases on occupational and managerial expertise, categories that are nearly empty in the aggregate marginals (1.4% and 3.1% respectively, Figures A6 and A10). Cluster 3 (N=6, 1.5%) contains, exactly, all six ministers with occupational expertise coded some (100% of the cluster, and 100% of the some-occupational marginal); its academic composition is mixed (16.7% none, 66.7% some, 16.7% ample) and its managerial expertise is low (mean 1.33). Cluster 2 (N=11, 2.7%) contains 11 of the 13 ministers with managerial expertise coded some (100% of the cluster’s managerial composition, and 85% of the some-managerial marginal, the remaining two falling in Cluster 3); its academic composition is also mixed (63.6% none, 36.4% some), and its occupational expertise is moderate (mean 2.09).
This is a structurally different clustering logic from Portugal’s. In Portugal, the five clusters read as genuine cross-cutting combinations of the three dimensions (for example, Polivalent Experts high on all three at once, Executive Politicians defined by ample managerial expertise regardless of the other two). In Spain, given how rare the some category is for occupational and managerial expertise, the automatic solution instead separates along academic level first (three pure academic-anchored clusters), then carves out two small residual clusters whose entire reason for existing is to isolate the scarce some cases on the other two dimensions, rather than representing a distinct substantive profile in their own right. This reading follows from cross-referencing the Figure C4 means with the Appendix composition tables; it should be confirmed against the actual model output before being finalized for publication.




Step 5: Cluster labeling — Data Manager task only (after Figure C4 is interpreted)

title: Report on Portfolio Expertise
section: Figure C5: Clusters vs. logical types
text:
Figure C5: Clusters vs. logical types
Cluster 5 draws primarily on academic-anchored logical types: integrated expertise (ample on all three, 40.5%), academic-occupational (29.8%), and academic-managerial (15.5%), together accounting for 85.8% of the cluster, plus a residual 14.3% pure academic. Cluster 1 is dominated by no expertise (43.8%, the only cluster where this type appears at meaningful scale, echoing Portugal’s Cluster 4 Academic Specialists) alongside managerial (21.9%) and occupational (18.5%) pure types; unlike Portugal, partial expertise is entirely absent from Cluster 1 (0.0%), which is itself informative: in Spain, the academic-floor cluster splits cleanly between nothing at all and ample on exactly one other dimension, with none of the flatter, moderate-everywhere profile that characterized Portugal’s analogous clusters. Cluster 4 is dominated by partial expertise (19.9%) together with occupational (30.9%) and occupational-managerial (32.4%) pure types, consistent with its moderately high occupational mean. Cluster 3 (the occupational-some residual) is 83.3% partial expertise plus 16.7% academic, consistent with its low managerial and mixed academic composition. Cluster 2 (the managerial-some residual) is 54.5% occupational plus 45.5% partial expertise, with no academic-anchored types at all, consistent with its complete absence of academic-ample cases.
As in Portugal, the empirical typology adds real resolution beyond the logical typology (three of five clusters are not simply pure logical types), but the underlying logic differs: Portugal’s residual clusters were dominated by partial expertise in a genuinely flat, moderate sense; Spain’s academic-anchored clusters (Cluster 1, Cluster 4) instead separate no-expertise from single-dimension-ample types quite cleanly, while partial expertise concentrates disproportionately in the two small some-isolating clusters (Cluster 2, Cluster 3). Cluster labels are not yet assigned for Spain (see Step 5 note); the readings above use cluster number only, as in the current cluster_final_label output.
